items.prompt: What does 'total cost of ownership' (TCO) mean?
choices: Every cost of an option over its life
The price printed on the vendor's invoice
The one-time cost of getting version one live
The yearly salary of the engineers building it
items.explanation: TCO adds up build, run, compliance, opportunity and exit costs over the whole lifetime.

items.prompt: A vendor fee shows up on an invoice. What kind of cost is that?
choices: A hidden, one-time cost
A visible, recurring cost
A cost that only exists for building
A cost that never grows
items.explanation: It is easy to see every month, which is why it dominates conversations.

items.prompt: Which of these is a cost of building that no invoice shows?
choices: A monthly subscription fee billed by a vendor
A per-transaction fee charged by a vendor
On-call and patches paid in salary time
A contract renewal charge from a vendor
items.explanation: Maintenance and on-call are paid in salary time, so they stay invisible in a fee comparison.

items.prompt: What is 'opportunity cost' in a build decision?
choices: The fee paid to a vendor each year
The cost of a failed compliance audit
The price of buying more servers
What the engineers could have built
items.explanation: Time spent on plumbing is time not spent on the product.

items.prompt: Which option usually has the higher exit cost?
choices: Building, since the code is yours to change
Buying, if tangled into the vendor
Neither, because exit is always free of cost
Building, since nobody else can read the code
items.explanation: Owned code can be changed freely; vendor-specific workflows are costly to untangle.

items.prompt: Why is 'two engineers for six months' an incomplete build price?
choices: It leaves out the years of running it
It counts each engineer twice by mistake
It assumes six months is always too long
It treats hired engineers as costing nothing
items.explanation: Most of a system's life is spent running, not building.

items.prompt: A team compares a yearly fee to a one-time build quote. What is wrong with that comparison?
choices: The fee is always the cheaper of the two options
A quote can never be compared to anything else
A recurring cost is set against a partial one
One-time costs are always the larger kind
items.explanation: Both sides need pricing over the same period and with the same line items.

items.prompt: Which line belongs in a TCO for both build and buy?
choices: The CEO's travel budget
The color of the dashboard
Office rent for the whole company
Compliance and security burden
items.explanation: Someone carries compliance either way: you, or the vendor and, partly, you.

items.prompt: A team says building 'saves the whole $396,000 fee'. Which flaw in that claim matters most?
choices: It ignores salaries and audits needed to run it
It prices the fee in the wrong currency
It assumes the vendor will soon lower its price
It counts the fee for too few years of use
items.explanation: Building replaces the fee with run costs; the saving is only the difference between the two.
items.reference:
Sticker price vs. total cost
🧾 the fee is the part you can see on an invoice
👩‍💻 salaries, audits and on-call are the parts you cannot
🎯 the engineers' alternative work is a cost too
🚪 leaving later is a cost too
Why: total cost of ownership prices every cost of an option over its whole life, so two options are compared on the same footing.
items.learnMore:
TCO is the whole bill, not the visible line

Both options have a visible cost and several hidden ones. Comparing a vendor's invoice to six months of salary compares a recurring visible number with a partial hidden one.

Common mistake

Treating the build as finished when the first version ships.
items.reflection: Think of a big purchase in your own life (a car, a subscription you could replace with a DIY setup). Which costs did you only notice after the first month?

items.prompt: Two proposals both total $2M over 3 years, but one is mostly upfront and one is mostly recurring. What does TCO tell you?
choices: The two proposals are identical in every way that matters
The recurring one is always the better choice here
The upfront one is always the better choice here
Totals match, but cash timing and risk still differ
items.explanation: TCO equalizes the sum, but when the money moves and who bears the risk still matter.

Payroll costs are only ever counted for vendor options

items.prompt: What makes a capability 'core'?
choices: It is technically difficult to build well
It is used by every team inside the company
Customers pick you because of it
It costs the most to run each year
items.explanation: Core is about the customer's choice, not about difficulty.

items.prompt: What is a 'context' capability?
choices: Something nobody in the company ever needs
Anything that was built a long time ago
Any capability that happens to use a database
Necessary, but not why customers pick you
items.explanation: Context is plumbing every company in your position needs.

items.prompt: A food-delivery app needs a map display. Is it likely core or context?
choices: Context, unless the map is the differentiator
Core, because maps are such a visual feature
Core, because every app has one on screen
Neither, because apps never need to show maps
items.explanation: Customers choose the app for food and speed, not for how the map is drawn.

items.prompt: A photo app's whole pitch is a unique background-removal model. Core or context?
choices: Context, since it is only a piece of software
Core, as the model is why people choose it
Context, since AI is now common everywhere
Neither, since models cannot really be owned
items.explanation: The model is the product's differentiator.

items.prompt: Which lean does 'context' point to, all else equal?
choices: Build
Buy
Wait
Stop
items.explanation: A specialist already did the work and carries the upkeep.

items.prompt: Which lean does 'core' point to?
choices: Buy
Wait
Stop
Build
items.explanation: Owning a differentiator lets you improve it without anyone's permission.

items.prompt: Can a capability be context for you and core for a vendor?
choices: Yes, payments are core only for a payment company
No, a capability has one fixed label forever
Yes, but only for vendors with a recognisable logo
No, vendors never treat anything as core
items.explanation: The label depends on what each company sells.

items.prompt: Is 'hard to build' the same as 'core'?
choices: Yes, hard things are always core ones
Yes, whenever a build takes over a month
No, hard things are often context
No, hard things are never ever important
items.explanation: Difficulty and differentiation are separate axes.

items.prompt: A company is proud that its checkout page is technically excellent underneath. Customers rarely mention it. What does the core test say?
choices: Core, since technical excellence always differentiates a product
Core, since checkout is a feature used by every customer
Neither, since the quality of checkout cannot be measured
Context: customers do not switch for it
items.explanation: The test asks whether customers would switch, not whether the work is impressive.
items.reference:
Core vs. context
⭐ core: customers choose you because of it
🔧 context: needed, but nobody picks you for it
🔎 ask: if we did this better than anyone, would people switch?
🏪 a vendor's core can be your context
Why: owning only the capabilities that differentiate you puts scarce engineering time where it changes the customer's choice.
items.learnMore:
Core means differentiating

Importance and difficulty do not make something core. What matters is whether doing it better wins you customers.

Common mistake

Calling something core because it is hard or critical.
items.reflection: Name something your team or household does that you could hand to a specialist without anyone noticing a drop in quality. What makes it 'context' for you?

items.prompt: A team argues a system is core 'because the whole company depends on it'. What is the flaw?

Being depended on is not the same as differentiating
Only very small systems can ever be called core
Core systems can never be relied on by others
items.explanation: Everything depends on login, yet no customer picks a company for its login.

items.prompt: What is vendor lock-in?
choices: Any use of a vendor's product at all
A high cost or delay in switching away
A contract that forbids anyone reading the code
The vendor's right to raise its prices
items.explanation: Lock-in is about the price of the exit.

items.prompt: Does using a vendor for five years automatically mean you are locked in?
choices: No, it depends on how tangled you are
Yes, long use always locks you in
Yes, but only after seven full years
No, lock-in only happens to large companies
items.explanation: Time matters less than the depth of dependence.

items.prompt: Which makes lock-in worse?
choices: Keeping the vendor behind a thin interface layer
Storing the data in an open, exportable format
Vendor-specific features throughout the code
Writing down exactly how a switch would work
items.explanation: The more of your code speaks the vendor's dialect, the more rewriting an exit needs.

items.prompt: Which reduces lock-in?
choices: Using every proprietary feature available
Never documenting the integration
Signing the longest possible contract
Keeping data in a format you can export
items.explanation: Portable data shortens the exit.

items.prompt: When should exit cost enter the build-versus-buy math?
choices: Only on the day someone proposes leaving
From the start, in the buy column
Never, it cannot be estimated
Only after the contract is signed
items.explanation: A cost you will probably pay later should be priced now.

items.prompt: What kinds of things become tangled with a vendor over time?
choices: Only the logo shown on invoices
Only the vendor's support phone number
Only the colors used on a dashboard
Data, workflows and team knowledge
items.explanation: These are the things that must move when you leave.

items.prompt: Is the exit cost for a build option usually high or low?
choices: High, because nobody else can run it
Always identical to the cost of buying
Low, since the system is already yours
Impossible to estimate before it happens
items.explanation: You can change or replace your own code without anyone's approval.

items.prompt: A team keeps its vendor behind a small wrapper layer. What does that mainly lower?
choices: The cost of switching vendors later
The vendor's monthly fee itself
The number of customers served
The need for any testing at all
items.explanation: Only the wrapper must change when the vendor changes.

items.prompt: A team uses a database vendor's proprietary query extensions in most of its code. What is the lock-in risk?
choices: None, because queries are cheap and quick to change
Every query using them needs a rewrite on exit
The vendor must approve each query before it ships
Only new queries are affected, and old ones are safe
items.explanation: Vendor-specific syntax spreads through the codebase, so the exit cost scales with its use.
items.reference:
Lock-in = cost of the way out
🔌 day 1: a light integration
🧵 years later: data, workflows and habits tied to the vendor
💸 the exit cost is what you pay to leave
📒 count it in the buy column from the start
Why: the more your product depends on a vendor's specifics, the more it costs to leave, even when leaving is clearly right.
items.learnMore:
Lock-in is switching cost, not usage

Using a vendor is not lock-in. Lock-in is how expensive and slow the exit would be.

Common mistake

Assuming that long use alone means you are locked in.
items.reflection: Think of a tool, app or service you rely on. If it vanished tomorrow, how long would the move to an alternative take, and what would you lose?

items.prompt: Why can a short relationship still involve heavy lock-in?
choices: Lock-in depends only on how long the contract runs
Short relationships can never lock anyone in
Dependence on specifics can grow within months
Lock-in is decided by how large the vendor is
items.explanation: Lock-in tracks depth of dependence, not duration.

items.prompt: In L2's test, which question comes first?
choices: What does the vendor charge each year?
How many engineers do we have free?
How long will the build take to finish?
Is it core to why customers choose you?
items.explanation: Classification comes before any price.

items.prompt: A capability is context. What is the next question?
choices: Does a mature vendor already exist?
Which engineer wants to build it?
What is the planned build timeline?
What did our competitors pick?
items.explanation: If a good vendor exists, buying follows.

items.prompt: A capability is core. What does the test suggest?
choices: Buy the cheapest option available
Postpone it for about a year
Build it and get it exactly right
Split it among three separate vendors
items.explanation: Core is worth owning.

items.prompt: A capability is context and no mature vendor exists. What does the test suggest?
choices: Buy anyway from the nearest vendor
Build reluctantly or wait
Mark it core and move on
Cancel the whole project
items.explanation: You pay an early-market tax either way.

items.prompt: Why does payment processing route to 'buy' for most companies?
choices: It is context and good vendors exist
It is always cheaper than building it
It is too small a job to build
It is not legal to build in-house
items.explanation: Both gates point the same way.

items.prompt: A company's entire product is a plagiarism detector. Build or buy the detection engine?
choices: Buy, because detection is a common feature
Buy, because engines are cheap to license
Build, since the engine is the product
Neither, because it cannot really be done
items.explanation: It passes the core test.

items.prompt: Does price play any role in the test?
choices: No, price is irrelevant to the test
Yes, but later, for how much and when
Yes, it is always the very first question
Only for capabilities labelled core
items.explanation: Price shapes the size of the commitment, not the category.

items.prompt: Which phrase describes what 'core' means precisely?
choices: It is important to the company
It is hard to build well
It runs around the clock every day
Doing it better would win you customers
items.explanation: The definition ties core to customer choice.

items.prompt: A logistics company's login system is critical, but its routing is why customers pick it. What does the test say about login?
choices: Core, because everything else in the company depends on it
Core, because it handles sensitive passwords for users
Neither, because login needs no category at all
Context: critical, but not why customers pick it
items.explanation: Critical and core are different axes.
items.reference:
Two questions, in order
1️⃣ is it core to why customers choose us?
✅ yes: build and get it exactly right
2️⃣ no: does a mature vendor already exist?
✅ yes: buy · ⚠️ no: build reluctantly or wait
Why: classifying the capability first prevents price from deciding a question that is really about where your effort matters.
items.learnMore:
Classify first, price second

The decision tree has two gates. Price enters later, to decide how much and when, not whether.

Common mistake

Starting from the cheapest number and working backwards.
items.reflection: Take a decision you made recently that started with price. What would the 'is this core to us?' question have changed?

Ignore the capability entirely until it eventually breaks
items.explanation: The second gate is about maturity, not just existence.

items.prompt: Why do build and buy cost curves cross?
choices: Both grow at exactly the same pace
Buy is flat while build keeps growing
Neither one depends on volume at all
Build is mostly fixed while buy grows
items.explanation: A flat line and a rising line must meet somewhere.

items.prompt: In this unit's model, what does a vendor's fee depend on?
choices: A percentage of payment volume
The number of engineers hired
The color of the checkout page
The month of the year
items.explanation: The assumed fee is 3.3% of volume.

items.prompt: At very low volume, which option is usually cheaper?
choices: Build, since fixed costs are tiny
Buy, since the fee is small
They always cost the same
Neither is ever cheaper
items.explanation: A small percentage of a small volume stays below build's fixed cost.

items.prompt: At very high volume, which option tends to win?
choices: Buy, since fees shrink as volume rises
Neither, since they become exactly equal
Build, since its fixed cost matters less
Buy, since vendors never charge more at scale
items.explanation: The percentage fee keeps rising while build stays flat.

items.prompt: What does the crossing point on the chart represent?
choices: The volume where the vendor goes out of business
The cheapest volume anywhere on the chart
The volume where the build work is finished
The volume where both options cost the same
items.explanation: Left of it one option is cheaper, right of it the other.

items.prompt: The model's 3-year build cost is $2,050,000. Does it change if volume doubles?
choices: Yes, it doubles with volume
Yes, it halves with volume
No, it is fixed in this model
Yes, it matches the vendor fee
items.explanation: Build's cost is set by setup and run cost, not by volume in this model.

items.prompt: Which two things can move the crossing point?
choices: Only the vendor's company logo
Volume of interest and the time horizon
Only the hair color of the founder
Neither one can move the crossing point
items.explanation: Extending years changes how much fixed setup is spread out.

items.prompt: Is the cheaper option today guaranteed to stay cheaper?
choices: No, growth can flip it
Yes, forever
Yes, if the vendor is large
No, but only if prices fall
items.explanation: Healthy growth pushes a company across the crossover.

items.prompt: At $2M a year, buy is clearly cheaper over 3 years ($198,000 vs. $2,050,000). What does that alone tell you about $40M?
choices: Buy stays cheaper at every volume
Nothing: at $40M, buy is $3,960,000
Build is cheaper at every volume
Buy and build both cost $198,000
items.explanation: The cost lines cross, so a verdict at one point does not hold at another.
items.reference:
Fixed cost vs. growing fee
📏 build: close to a flat line
📈 buy: rises with volume
✖️ they cross at about $20.7M a year (3-year, assumed rates)
↔️ below it buy wins, above it build wins
Why: build's cost is mostly fixed while a usage fee scales with volume, so the cheaper option depends on where you are on that axis.
items.learnMore:
A crossover, not a winner

Neither option is cheaper everywhere. The verdict depends on volume and the time horizon you pick.

Common mistake

Judging both options at today's volume only.
items.reflection: Think of a subscription versus buying outright, such as renting a tool versus owning it. How much use would flip your answer?

items.prompt: With the assumed 3.3% fee, about what yearly volume equalizes 3-year buy with the $2,050,000 build?
choices: About $20.7M a year
About $2.07M a year
About $207M a year
About $6.2M a year
items.explanation: $2,050,000 divided by (0.033 x 3) is about $20.7M.
items.reference:
Fixed cost vs. growing fee
📏 build: close to a flat line
📈 buy: rises with volume
✖️ they cross at about $20.7M a year (3-year, assumed rates)
↔️ below it buy wins, above it build wins
Why: build's cost is mostly fixed while a usage fee scales with volume, so the cheaper option depends on where you are on that axis.
items.learnMore:
A crossover, not a winner

Neither option is cheaper everywhere. The verdict depends on volume and the time horizon you pick.

Common mistake

Judging both options at today's volume only.
items.reflection: Think of a subscription versus buying outright, such as renting a tool versus owning it. How much use would flip your answer?

items.prompt: In the L3 model, what is the one-time setup cost?
items.explanation: Setup is build engineering, first certification and initial fraud tooling.

items.prompt: In the L3 model, what is the yearly run cost?
items.explanation: Engineers, audits, on-call and fraud upkeep total $450,000.

items.prompt: What is year 1's build cost in the model?
items.explanation: Setup plus one year of run cost.

items.prompt: What is each of years 2 and 3?
items.explanation: Only the run cost remains.

items.prompt: What is the 3-year build total?
items.explanation: $1,150,000 plus two years of $450,000.

items.prompt: Why is year 1 higher than year 3?
choices: Salaries drop by half in year 3
Audits stop once year 1 is over
The vendor lowers its fee in year 3
Year 1 includes the one-time setup
items.explanation: The gap is the $700,000 entry fee.

items.prompt: Which line in the run cost is the largest?
choices: Engineers maintaining it, $250,000
On-call allowance, $50,000
Fraud tooling upkeep, $30,000
Annual audit, $120,000 each year
items.explanation: Maintenance is the biggest recurring line.

items.prompt: Are the model's figures real market prices?
choices: Yes, taken from published vendor price lists
Yes, taken from an audit report
No, they are illustrative assumptions
Yes, set by a regulator
items.explanation: The unit labels them as assumptions.

items.prompt: Year 4 is added to the model with no change in assumptions. What should it cost?
choices: About $1,150,000, the same as year 1
About $225,000, half of year 3
About $450,000, the same as year 3
About $700,000, the setup again
items.explanation: Setup was one-time, so year 4 is run cost only.
items.reference:
Setup once, run every year
🏗️ setup (year 1 only): $700,000
🔁 run: $450,000 each year
1️⃣ year 1: $1,150,000
3️⃣ three years: $2,050,000
Why: pricing build as setup plus run cost explains why year 1 is the most expensive and why later years are flat.
items.learnMore:
Split one-time from recurring

A build has a one-time setup and a recurring run cost. The two behave differently over a long horizon, so they need separate lines.

Common mistake

Spreading setup evenly and calling year 1 average.
items.reflection: Think of a project you started where the first month was the most expensive. What part was a one-time fee and what part kept recurring?

items.explanation: The total is the same, but cash timing and the case for stopping early differ.

items.prompt: What is the model for, when totals are nearly tied?
choices: Which assumptions the decision rests on
A single winner, named by one dollar
A replacement for all human judgment
Proof that the vendor is wrong
items.explanation: Sensitivity to assumptions is what the model reveals.

items.prompt: The rate is renegotiated from 3.3% to 2.8% on the same $62M. What is buy's new 3-year total?
items.reference:
What the near-tie leaves out
💳 2,046,000 (buy) vs. 2,050,000 (build): a $4,000 gap
📉 a lower negotiated rate favors buy
🕵️ weaker home-grown fraud tools favor buy
🚪 exit cost sits on the buy side
Why: when totals are this close, unpriced items decide, so the model's job is to show which assumptions matter, not to name a winner.
items.learnMore:
A near-tie is a prompt to look elsewhere

If the totals nearly match, the decision hinges on what the model does not price: rates, quality, failure ownership and exit.

Common mistake

Treating a $4,000 difference as a decisive result.
items.reflection: Take a decision where two options came out nearly equal. Which unpriced factor ended up deciding it, and could you have listed it beforehand?
